ORIGINAL USMLE-STYLE PRACTICE

shoulder imaging — clinical pattern 1

A patient has a deformed shoulder after forced abduction and external rotation. Orthogonal imaging shows the humeral head anterior and inferior to the glenoid in a subcoracoid position, without a surgical-neck fracture. Which alignment abnormality is present?

  1. Posterior glenohumeral dislocation
  2. Inferior glenohumeral dislocation
  3. Acromioclavicular separation
  4. Proximal humeral surgical-neck fracture
  5. Anterior glenohumeral dislocation
Answer and explanation

Anterior glenohumeral dislocation

The humeral head lies anterior to the glenoid, commonly in a subcoracoid position.

Option explanations

Anterior glenohumeral dislocation: The humeral head lies anterior to the glenoid, commonly in a subcoracoid position.

Posterior glenohumeral dislocation: Axillary or another appropriate orthogonal view shows the humeral head behind the glenoid; AP imaging alone may miss it. This is not the pattern specified in this case.

Inferior glenohumeral dislocation: The humeral head lies below the glenoid, often with the arm fixed overhead. This is not the pattern specified in this case.

Acromioclavicular separation: The distal clavicle is displaced relative to the acromion while the glenohumeral joint remains located. This is not the pattern specified in this case.

Proximal humeral surgical-neck fracture: A fracture below the tuberosities separates the shaft from the proximal humeral segment. This is not the pattern specified in this case.
